overview.text: Exponentiation, also called raising to a power, is an arithmetic operation written with a base and a smaller, raised exponent: in 3⁴, 3 is the base and 4 the exponent. For a positive whole-number exponent, it means multiplying the base by itself that many times, so 3⁴ = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81. This compact notation records repeated multiplication. It also extends beyond that basic case: for a nonzero base, a zero exponent gives 1, while a negative exponent represents a reciprocal. Exponents matter when reading expressions, too: in standard order of operations, powers are evaluated before multiplication and addition.

key_facts.text: In aⁿ, a is the base and n is the exponent; the exponent is written above and to the right of the base.
For a positive whole-number exponent, 2³ means 2 × 2 × 2, which equals 8.
For a nonzero base a, a⁰ = 1; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.
When multiplying powers with the same base, add the exponents: aⁿ × aᵐ = aⁿ⁺ᵐ.
In standard order of operations, exponents are evaluated before multiplication, division, addition, and subtraction.
